TEAs are a means of evaluating the cost and performance of a technology and are developed for a variety of purposes, including establish a commercial benchmark, estimate the commercial potential of a technology, inform research, development, and demonstration (RD&D) priorities, inform business or policy decisions, and assess economic uncertainty and risk. LCA can be used to determine the environmental impacts of a process, including contributions outside of the plant gate. The goal is to present results in a consistent and transparent manner, following National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL) Quality Guidelines for Energy System Studies (QGESS) documents, wherever applicable. Three study cases were selected for analysis. One plant configuration, natural gas steam methane reforming (SMR) without CCS (Case 1), represents the most common way ammonia is produced in the United States today. The other two plant configurations, natural gas SMR with CCS (Case 2) and natural gas autothermal reforming (ATR) with CCS (Case 3), represent options for ammonia production that reduce stack CO emissions. Study cases reflect the capabilities of 2 current, commercial technologies at scales representative of next commercial offerings facing no fundamental RD&D obstacles. The balance of the report is organized as follows: • Design Basis – details assumptions for performance, cost, and life cycle modeling for the study cases • Study Cases – provides information on the process description, performance modeling, and cost estimating for three study cases • Results & Discussion – compares performance, life cycle, and cost results of the study cases and explores how various parameters affect the cost results in sensitivity analyses • Conclusion – summarizes key study results and takeaways and includes a discussion of follow-on analyses that could provide additional insights 1.1 LITERATURE REVIEW A literature review was conducted to inform the study case selection process.
